title: Global Entry Renewal: My Step-By-Step Experience, Cost, And Timeline
summary: Renewing Global Entry took about 15 minutes online and approval came 10 days later, with no interview. Here's the step-by-step process, what it costs, and when to renew.
content: Global Entry is an incredibly useful program for anyone who travels internationally with any frequency. I’ve had Global Entry for nearly 15 years now. Several weeks ago, I received an email reminding me that I was within six months of my Global Entry expiring, so I just went through the process of renewing it. In this post, I’d like to outline the process of renewing a Global Entry membership, since it’s something that frequent travelers have to do periodically. I’ll include a step-by-step guide, the cost, and the timeline. I’ve separately written about how to apply for Global Entry . What is Global Entry? For those not familiar, Global Entry is a US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) program that allows expedited clearance for pre-approved, low-risk travelers upon arrival in the United States (or at CBP Preclearance facilities ). With this program, approved members can enter the United States using their biometric data at virtually all international airports . The exact way that biometric data is verified varies by airport. It used to be that you’d have to go up to one of the Global Entry kiosks and answer a few questions. Then they updated the technology, and you just had to stand in front of one of those kiosks for a few seconds. Now many airports just have a camera in the Global Entry lane that automatically verifies your identity as you walk through. It’s pretty awesome. You do still typically have to walk past an immigration officer and verify that you don’t have anything to declare. You can then proceed to the baggage claim area and exit (unless you’re selected for additional screening ). Over the years, Global Entry has probably saved me dozens of hours. Back in the day I’d be stressed when landing back in the United States, wondering if I’d be stuck in an hour-long immigration queue. Nowadays I can just breeze right through. Global Entry is incredibly valuable for international travelers Global Entry renewal process, timeline, and cost Before I share a step-by-step guide of my Global Entry renewal experience, let me share some basics about the timeline, how much it costs, etc. How long is Global Entry valid for? Global Entry is valid for roughly five years after you’re approved. The reason I say “roughly” is because it’s valid for five years from your next birthday. In other words, if your birthday is December 1, and you apply January 1, 2027, your membership would be valid through December 1, 2032. If you strategically apply for Global Entry, you can get it for almost six years with one membership. Just apply shortly after your birthday. How do you determine when your Global Entry expires? Generally speaking you’ll get an email six months before your Global Entry expires informing you of the upcoming expiration. If you want to look for it in your email, that usually comes from donotreply@cbp.dhs.gov. Alternatively you can log into your Trusted Traveler Program dashboard , and go to the section that lists your program status. You’ll see the expiration date listed there. Global Entry dashboard When can you renew your Global Entry? You can apply to have your Global Entry renewed up to a year before the expiration date. There’s no penalty for renewing early, in the sense that it will still be valid for five years from when your membership currently expires, and not five years from when you’re approved. So you might as well renew early. You won’t want to let your membership lapse, since the process is more complicated for a lapsed membership. Be sure to apply for renewal well before your Global Entry is set to expire. Is there a grace period for Global Entry renewal? There is a grace period for Global Entry renewal, as long as you submit your renewal application before your membership expires. Specifically, there’s a grace period of up to 24 months, which is super long. Back in the day, the grace period was only six months, but that has been increased considerably over time. If you do submit your application but aren’t approved before the expiration, you’ll continue to be able to use Global Entry the same way as before during that period. How much does it cost to renew Global Entry? It costs $120 for adults to renew Global Entry (Global Entry is free for kids under the age of 18 ). Fortunately, many credit cards offer a fee credit toward Global Entry renewal. Note that in all cases, you can use your credit for anyone — so if you have extra credits, you can use them for friends and family to renew their Global Entry. Do you have to be interviewed for Global Entry renewal? When you first apply for Global Entry you have to be interviewed, either in-person or virtually. Do you need to be interviewed when you renew? It depends: Some people who apply for renewal get a full approval without having to attend an in-person interview Some people who apply for renewal have to attend an interview The good news is that if you do need to attend an interview, you can simply do so when you return to the United States with your next trip What happens to Global Entry if your passport expires? While only tangentially related, what happens if you have to renew your passport before your Global Entry expires? The good news is that it’s a really easy process. You just have to log into your account on the Trusted Traveler Programs website and update your passport number there. Your Global Entry will then continue to apply with the new passport up until the Global Entry expiration date. See this post for more details on how that works. Step-by-step guide to renewing Global Entry On November 15, 2026, I submitted my application to renew Global Entry. My current membership expires on April 20, 2027, though as long as the application is submitted before then, there’s a grace period of two years. To renew your Global Entry membership, you’ll want to go to the Trusted Traveler Programs website , and click “LOG IN” at the top right under the “Returning GE/NEXUS/SENTRI/FAST Member/Applicants” heading. Global Entry renewal process Note that back in 2017 the government migrated from the Global Online Enrollment System (GOES). So if you don’t yet have a new Trusted Traveler Programs profile, you’ll have to set that up first, which is a quick process (though at this point I imagine that virtually everyone has transitioned). Global Entry renewal process Once logged in you’ll see your current Global Entry membership, and underneath that you should see a “Renew Membership” option listed, assuming you’re within the renewal period. Global Entry renewal process There you’ll be able to select the program you want to apply for or renew, which in this case would be Global Entry. Global Entry renewal process Essentially the Global Entry renewal application contains all the information you submitted the last time around, so you just have to confirm that it’s correct, and update any outdated information. Global Entry renewal process This includes reviewing your personal information, documents, driver’s license, address, employment info, travel history, and more. Global Entry renewal process You do have to upload a copy of your passport during the process (assuming your passport number changed since your last application, which will likely be the case half of the time for adults, since passports are usually valid for 10 years, while Global Entry is valid for five or so years). Global Entry renewal process The only slightly complicated part of this process is having to update your travel history, as you have to list all of the countries that you’ve been to since the last time that you applied. So yeah, that can take a second, if you’re a frequent traveler. Global Entry renewal process Global Entry renewal process At some points the process of reviewing info isn’t very intuitive, as you have to click a lot of unnecessary buttons confirming that nothing has changed. But it’s pretty self explanatory. I’d say the whole process up until this point took me about 15 minutes, and that includes having to recall all the countries from the past five years (which is quite a few). To finish off the process you just have to certify that all of the information that you’re providing is accurate, and then you have to pay. Global Entry renewal process When you pay, make sure you use a credit card that has a Global Entry fee credit, assuming you have one. Global Entry renewal process I used my Amex Business Platinum, and the fee reimbursed within two days. Global Entry renewal fee reimbursement How long did the Global Entry renewal take? As mentioned above, I submitted the Global Entry renewal application on November 15, 2026. Then on November 25, 2026 — 10 days later — I received an email indicating that there had been an application status change on the renewal. The email came from noreplyttp4@cbp.dhs.gov with the subject line “TTP Application Status Change.” The email as such doesn’t tell you a whole lot, so you have to log into your account again to see the status. There I found out that the application was approved, meaning that there was no need to take part in an interview. Experiences seem to be mixed as to whether an interview is required for renewals. For example, during my last renewal, I did need to get an interview, while during my renewal before that, I didn’t need to get an interview. The good news is that if you do need to be interviewed, you can typically just do so when you return from an international trip. When I did it, it took less than a minute. Global Entry renewal approval Bottom line I just went through the process of renewing Global Entry, and it was pretty easy. You basically just have to confirm that all the information during your last application is still accurate, add all the countries you’ve been to since then, and pay a fee. This time around, the application was processed in 10 days, and there was a full approval, so no interview was required. However, don’t be surprised if you do need an interview, as that happened to me during my last renewal. Hopefully this is useful for anyone else who has a Global Entry renewal coming up soon. If you’ve had to renew your Global Entry, what was your experience like?

title: Hyatt Credit Cards Compared: Is The Personal Or Business Card Better?
summary: Chase offers one personal and one business World of Hyatt card. Here's how they compare, and why the personal card is easier to justify, though you can hold both.
content: Chase and Hyatt have a pretty straightforward co-brand card portfolio, as there’s one personal card and one business card. Specifically, I’m talking about the World of Hyatt Credit Card and the World of Hyatt Business Credit Card. In this post, I’d like to compare the two cards, and talk about which is better. First let’s cover the details of both products, and then I’ll share my take on which is worth applying for. This is an especially good time to pick them up, given the current welcome offers. Link: Learn more about the World of Hyatt Credit Card or World of Hyatt Business Credit Card The details of Hyatt’s two co-branded credit cards To start, let’s cover the details of Hyatt’s two co-branded credit cards. Below is a chart with the basics, and I’ll go into a bit more detail below. Card feature World of Hyatt Card World of Hyatt Business Card Annual fee $95 $199 Elite status Discoverist for as long as you hold the card Discoverist for you plus up to five employees Elite nights (no spend) Five qualifying nights each year None Elite nights from spending Two nights per $5,000 spent, uncapped (one night per $2,500) Five nights per $10,000 spent in a calendar year, uncapped (one night per $2,000) Free night awards One Category 1–4 anniversary night, plus a second after $15,000 spend in a calendar year None Hyatt credits None Up to $100 per anniversary year ($50 back on a $50+ Hyatt purchase, twice) Points rebate None 10% back on redeemed points (up to 20,000/year) once you spend $50,000 in a calendar year Earning on Hyatt stays 4x points 4x points Earning on bonus categories 2x points on restaurants, airline tickets, gyms and fitness clubs, and local transit/commuting 2x points in your top three categories each quarter, from a set list Earning on everything else 1x points 1x points Best for Anyone who stays at Hyatt occasionally; it’s worth keeping for the perks, and it’s the strongest choice for $15K per year in spending Big spenders chasing Hyatt status, and anyone who wants the welcome bonus World of Hyatt Credit Card details The World of Hyatt Credit Card ( learn more ) is Hyatt’s personal credit card, with a $95 annual fee. Hyatt’s personal credit card offers a variety of perks, including the following: World of Hyatt Discoverist status for as long as you have the card Five elite qualifying nights every year just for having the card, plus two elite qualifying nights for every $5,000 spent on the card on an ongoing basis; this can help you earn World of Hyatt Explorist status , World of Hyatt Globalist status , and/or other Milestone Rewards An anniversary free night award valid at a Category 1-4 property, plus a second anniversary free night award when you spend $15,000 on the card in a calendar year 4x points on Hyatt spending, 2x points on restaurants, airline tickets, fitness clubs and gym memberships, and local transit and commuting, and 1x points on all other eligible purchases, with no foreign transaction fees Receive an anniversary free night award with the Hyatt Card World of Hyatt Business Credit Card details The World of Hyatt Business Credit Card ( learn more ) is Hyatt’s business credit card, with a $199 annual fee. Hyatt’s business credit card offers many benefits, including the following: World of Hyatt Discoverist status for as long as you have the card, plus the same status for up to five employees Five elite qualifying nights for every $10,000 spent on the card in a calendar year, with no limit Up to $100 in Hyatt credits annually, where when you spend $50 or more you’ll receive a $50 statement credit, up to two times; this is based on the anniversary year, and not the calendar year A 10% rebate on redeemed points, up to 20,000 points per year; you only unlock this if you spend $50,000 on the card in a calendar year, and the benefit applies for the remainder of the calendar year in which you complete the spending 4x points on Hyatt spending, 2x points in your top three spending categories from select options each quarter, and 1x points on all other eligible purchases, with no foreign transaction fees Spend your way to status with the Hyatt Business Card Which of Hyatt’s two credit cards is better? If you’re considering applying for a Hyatt credit card and would be eligible for a business or personal card, which should you apply for? The first thing to understand is that the World of Hyatt Card and World of Hyatt Business Card aren’t mutually exclusive. You could apply for both cards, and also earn the welcome bonus on each. So in some ways, it’s worth assessing the value of the cards independently, since you don’t actually have to decide between them. If you ask me, the World of Hyatt Card is a slam dunk if you stay at Hyatts with any frequency . The card has a reasonable annual fee, and it’s worth holding onto even if you don’t spend a dime on it. The annual free night award alone more than justifies the annual fee, and the five nights toward elite status with no spending requirement is a great perk as well. On top of that, I think there’s merit to spending $15,000 on the card per year, to earn a second annual free night award, plus to earn an additional six elite nights toward status. The math on the World of Hyatt Business Card isn’t quite as straightforward. The card has a different welcome bonus than on the personal card, so there’s merit to picking up the card for that. But beyond that, the main reason you’ll want to get this card is because it offers the best rate of return on spending in terms of earning elite nights. With the business card, you can earn one elite night for every $2,000 spent, while with the personal card, you can get one elite night for every $2,500 spent (though the increments for earning elite nights differ). So my best consolidated advice would be that the World of Hyatt Card is more valuable and is easier to justify, and is the best for the first $15,000 in spending annually. Beyond that, though, the World of Hyatt Business Card is best for helping to earn Hyatt status, especially if you’re a big spender. Furthermore, it can be worth picking up the card in part for the huge bonus. The personal card is easier to justify, in my opinion Bottom line Hyatt has both a personal and business co-branded credit cards. The products are totally different, and there’s potentially merit to both. The World of Hyatt Card is much easier to justify — the card has a lower annual fee, offers an annual free night award, provides five nights toward status without a spending requirement, and more. That being said, you don’t have to decide between the two cards, and there’s also merit to getting the World of Hyatt Business Card . The card has a better welcome bonus, and has the potential to be more rewarding for spending. What’s your take on the value proposition of Hyatt’s personal vs. business card?

title: Not Again: Cargo Jet Overruns Miami Airport Runway (This Time A FedEx MD-11)
summary: A FedEx MD-11 overran runway 26R at Miami on Wednesday evening, stopping near the perimeter fence. The pilots walked away, but the incident caused a nearly two-hour ground stop.
content: Miami International Airport (MIA) is having a bad luck streak when it comes to cargo planes being able to stay on the runway, but at least this time around there were no fatalities. Still, yikes… FedEx jet overruns runway, leading to Miami ground stop At 8:25PM on Wednesday, November 25, 2026, a FedEx McDonnell Douglas MD-11 overran the runway at Miami Airport, leading the airport to be shut down for an extended period of time. The 34-year-old MD-11 with the registration code N605FE had just performed flight FX910 from Memphis (MEM), and was coming in to land on runway 26R, which is 9,355 feet (2,851 meters) long. That’s a solidly long runway, for what it’s worth. However, the plane wasn’t able to stop before the end of the runway, and seemed to exit the paved surface at a speed of around 50 knots, and came to a stop around 320 meters (1,000 feet) past the end of the runway, right by the airport perimeter fence. 🚨 USA | FEDEX CARGO PLANE OVERRUNS RUNWAY AT #MIAMI AIRPORT! MD-11 arriving from Memphis skidded into the grass beyond Runway 26R, triggering an FAA ground stop. 2 crew members are safe. No deaths or injuries. #FlaPanthers #Survivor51 #ไฟไหม้ pic.twitter.com/kTM48GkeGf — Eyes on the Globe (@eyes_globe) November 26, 2026 WATCH: FedEx cargo plane in the grass after overshooting runway at Miami International Airport pic.twitter.com/t4DPQwUb0m — BNO News (@BNONews) November 26, 2026 Fortunately there were no serious injuries. There’s video footage showing stairs being pulled up to the plane, and the pilots walking off with their bags. There’s always the classic aviation adage that “any landing you can walk away from is a good one,” and if that’s the case, I guess this was a good landing. Footage showing the FedEx Express MD-11F after it overran the runway at Miami International Airport tonight. As a result of the incident, a ground stop was issued. pic.twitter.com/ldraejGQ4v — OSINTdefender (@sentdefender) November 26, 2026 This accident ended up causing a ground stop of nearly two hours at the airport. That’s not exactly ideal timing, given what a busy travel day yesterday was, ahead of Thanksgiving. Operations did eventually resume, but with delays averaging over three hours. 🚨 迈阿密国际机场关闭！ 今晚，一架联邦快递（FedEx）货运飞机在迈阿密国际机场（MIA）冲出跑道，机场目前已实施地面停飞令（Ground Stop）。 根据空中交通管制（ATC）的录音，飞机冲出跑道后，管制员通知其他飞行员，机场“刚刚关闭”。 这是今年迈阿密国际机场发生的第二起货运飞机冲出跑道事故。… — 花岗岩³ (@Granite77777) November 26, 2026 Of course the concept of a plane overrunning a runway at Miami Airport is fresh on people’s minds, given the September 6 accident we saw with a 21 Air (Amazon Air) Boeing 767-300 that overran runway 30. Tragically that accident claimed five lives, as the plane ran through the perimeter fence, and killed motorists. What we’ve found out about the piloting of that flight since the accident, and just how recklessly the captain was flying the plane , is astounding. What went wrong with this FedEx MD-11 in Miami? We’ll have to wait for a full investigation to know what happened (the NTSB typically releases a preliminary report within a month), but in terms of circumstances and possible contributing factors, there are a couple of things we know. First, there’s footage showing the plane’s approach, and it makes it pretty clear that the plane touched down extremely late. JUST IN: FedEx cargo plane overruns the runway at Miami International Airport. Flights halted pic.twitter.com/PFFH0TNpe1 — BNO News (@BNONews) November 26, 2026 A recreation of the approach based on flight tracking data shows just how late the plane touched down, and the big question is why the pilots didn’t perform a go around. 🚨 BREAKING: FedEx FDX910, an MD-11F registered N605FE, went off the end of runway 26R landing at Miami International from Memphis at about 8:28 PM local, Nov 25. Tower sent the next arrival around and ground control closed the airport. No injuries reported so far. pic.twitter.com/IhRUGEVR97 — Squawk (@UseSquawk) November 26, 2026 It’s also worth pointing out that weather in the region was really bad at the time of the accident. Anna Giaritelli, a reputable aviation journalist with good sources, quotes a Miami air traffic controller, who told her that “this was absolutely the most dangerous operation I’ve seen,” as much of the traffic approaching Miami had run into a “black hole of weather.” A Miami air traffic controller sent me this chilling text minutes before the FedEx incident in MIA tonight (Controller was not on duty while texting me.) pic.twitter.com/Fvy7vb7xuP — Anna Giaritelli (@Anna_Giaritelli) November 26, 2026 It doesn’t seem like conditions at Miami Airport as such were that awful (compared to reports of severe turbulence in the region), but I imagine the bad weather could’ve contributed to a sense of “get-there-itis” for the pilots . While this is of course unfortunate, the great news here is the lack of injuries or fatalities. The plane ended up coming to a stop just feet from the airport’s perimeter fence, and if it had crashed through that, the outcome could’ve been completely different, with fatalities among motorists. It also has to be acknowledged that the pilots seemingly turned the plane a little bit left off the end of the runway, to avoid the localizer antenna. So at least the overrun was handled as well as it could be. Based on the preliminary information we have so far, DEI does not appear to be a factor in this accident. 😉 Bottom line A FedEx MD-11 overran the runway at Miami Airport last night, and ended up in the grass just short of the airport perimeter fence. Fortunately there were no major injuries, and the pilots managed to walk off the plane. This had major operational impacts for the airport, as a ground stop was issued, delaying lots of travelers. Unlike the 21 Air Boeing 767 accident we saw in September, there were no fatalities this time around. Either way, two cargo planes going off Miami runways in under three months is not great. What do you make of this FedEx MD-11 accident in Miami?

title: Norse Atlantic Collapses: Airline Cancels Flights, Strands Passengers
summary: Hours after calling its financial situation critical, Norse Atlantic canceled its flights and stranded travelers, including Pakistan International Airlines passengers. Here's how the airline got here.
content: Back in August 2026, all-Boeing 787 airline Norse Atlantic Airways announced it was in a rough financial spot , and was pursuing a sale, merger, or other arrangement. Not a whole lot of progress was made in subsequent months, and just this morning, the airline announced that it was in a “critical” financial situation. Well, it seems that it didn’t take long for things to get much worse, as the airline has seemingly canceled all flights just hours later, leaving travelers stranded. The end is here for Norse Atlantic Airways, it seems Earlier today, Norse Atlantic provided an update on its financial situation and ongoing strategic review. There’s no point in paraphrasing this, so here’s the direct statement from the airline: The Company’s financial situation is critical. It is dependent on securing financing to meet its short-term liquidity needs and to continue its operations. Norse, supported by its advisors, has explored various strategic alternatives and entertains discussions for a potential takeover. In parallel, the Board and management have diligently considered other available options, including ACMI contracts. Norse is also engaged in discussions with selected parties on short term financing, however, there can be no assurances that such discussions will result in a viable solution. To state the obvious, this sounded really, really bad. When the company was publicly stating that its “financial situation is critical” and that it needed to secure financing to meet “short-term liquidity needs,” you knew things weren’t good. I expected we’d see something bad happen in the coming weeks, but it didn’t take that long. Norse Atlantic has canceled its own scheduled flights effective immediately. On top of that, the airline was leasing two jets to Pakistan International Airlines, and those flights were also canceled with very little notice, “due to an unexpected operational suspension” by Norse Atlantic. Travelers were literally checking in at the airport when they realized the airline was grounded. Due to an unexpected operational suspension by our wet-lease partner Norse Air without prior notice, tonight’s PK786 (London–Islamabad) & PK710 (Manchester–Lahore) are cancelled. We deeply regret the disruption. Efforts have been made to mitigate the impact, and from tomorrow,… — PIA (@Official_PIA) November 25, 2026 So while the company hasn’t formally announced that it’s liquidating, it’s clear that operations are at least suspended, and we’ll see how this all plays out. Norse Atlantic ceased operations with no notice What has gone wrong with Norse Atlantic Airways? The airline industry can be a funny business, and there’s no clearer example of that than Norse Atlantic Airways. The airline launched in 2022 , with the goal of operating long haul, low cost flights, particularly across the Atlantic. That wasn’t exactly a unique business model, because this was exactly what Norwegian did, before it discontinued long haul flights in 2021 . Not only was the idea sort of copied, but Norse Atlantic had some executives from Norwegian, and even picked up the planes that Norwegian previously flew. But as is all too common in the airline industry, clearly they thought it would be different this time around… it wasn’t. So in 2024 we saw the airline update its business model , making the focus less about operating regularly scheduled commercial flights, and more about leasing out aircraft, all while reducing its fleet. The company got a lifeline when IndiGo decided to lease some Norse Atlantic 787s to dabble in long haul flying, ahead of the airline taking delivery of its own Airbus A350s . However, between all the airspace closures, high oil costs, and generally declining performance at IndiGo as the airline increasingly moved away from its core strengths, the airline recently decided to scrap that experiment, and stop leasing planes from Norse Atlantic. Since then, opportunities for Norse Atlantic have been limited. The airline did manage to lease a couple of Dreamliners to the “new” Pakistan International Airlines , but for an airline with 12 planes, that hardly pays the bills. Norse Atlantic did still operate some of its own flights, but in a very limited capacity. The airline had some flights from Europe to Thailand, South Africa, and the United States, but most were seasonal, and they were a fraction of what they previously were. Clearly they just didn’t have enough money to “keep the lights on” anymore. I am curious to see what comes next for Norse Atlantic’s 787s. The airline doesn’t own them, but instead, they’ll presumably return to their leasing companies. I can’t help but point out that Southwest Airlines wants to start long haul flights . The airline had been considering a Boeing 787 order, and was possibly even looking at ways to get planes faster than from a direct order (which requires waiting for years). Could these dozen Norse Atlantic 787s somehow end up at Southwest? The interiors would just need some updates (assuming the airline wants to offer business class), but talk about a quick way to grow a decent sized fleet. Norse Atlantic’s top cabin is premium economy Bottom line This morning, Norse Atlantic released a statement admitting that its “financial situation is critical,” and that the company’s future is “dependent on securing financing to meet short-term liquidity needs.” That wasn’t exactly a great sign, but little did we know that the company would collapse just hours later, as the airline has now ceased all flying, including on a wet lease basis. Financial issues at the company started when… well, it launched. Norse Atlantic was just a direct replica of Norwegian, which had failed. When the airline realized that the long haul, low cost business model doesn’t really work, they tried to pivot to wet leasing. And while there’s some demand for that, it’s also not a 100% consistent business in terms of demand. I feel horribly for all the frontline employees at Norse Atlantic who put their best foot forward. May they find good opportunities at other airlines. What do you make of Norse Atlantic’s seeming collapse?

title: The Park Hyatt Beaver Creek Will Pay You To Redeem Points Over Peak Dates… But Why?
summary: Park Hyatt Beaver Creek is giving back 15,000 points per night on award stays over peak holiday dates. Here's how it works, and why the hotel would do this.
content: The Park Hyatt Beaver Creek is incentivizing people to redeem points at the property for stays over some pretty peak dates, which you don’t often see, as flagged by View from the Wing . This has the potential to be a good deal, but beyond that, I think the more interesting part of this story is the topic of why the hotel would offer something like this, since this is pretty rare. Unique Park Hyatt Beaver Creek award stay promotion The Park Hyatt Beaver Creek is offering 15,000 points back per night when you redeem over some peak dates, for a total of up to 90,000 points back (which you’d get if redeeming for six nights). To cover the basics: This applies to new points bookings made between November 25 and December 5, 2026 You must stay between December 18, 2026, and January 3, 2027 You must redeem at the full cost, and then email your reservation confirmation to beave-reservations.static@hyatt.com, to request the points back Existing reservations don’t qualify toward this offer Park Hyatt Beaver Creek points deal by u/David_Copperfield in hyatt The Park Hyatt Beaver Creek is a ski-in, ski-out property in Colorado, and it’s one I’ve reviewed before . For what it’s worth, the hotel is currently charging 55,000 World of Hyatt points per night over the dates eligible for this promotion. Based on my valuation of 1.4 cents per World of Hyatt point, that means a redemption will cost you the equivalent of $770 per night. Meanwhile cash rates are running double as much, and that’s before taxes are factored in. Park Hyatt Beaver Creek points rate Park Hyatt Beaver Creek cash rate Why the Park Hyatt Beaver Creek wants points redemptions Understandably, I think a lot of people might be confused as to why the Park Hyatt Beaver Creek would be incentivizing award redemptions in this way. If the hotel wants to fill rooms, why only offer bonus points for points stays, and not for cash stays? That’s especially true when you consider redeeming points is already a good value compared to the cash rate. The explanation here is probably pretty simple, if you understand the economics at play. I’ve written in the past about how hotels are reimbursed for award stays . Keep in mind that the loyalty program centrally (rather than the individual hotel) sets the cost for redemptions, based on their internal costs associated with redemptions. The way it generally works is as follows: When a hotel isn’t full, the loyalty program compensates the hotel at a pre-determined rate that’s above the marginal cost of accommodating a guest, but hardly lucrative for the hotel When a hotel is full (think 90-95%+ occupancy), the loyalty program compensates the hotel at close to the average daily rate, in recognition of the fact that the room may have otherwise been sold to a guest paying with cash How does this all factor into the Park Hyatt Beaver Creek’s promotion? I suspect a few factors are at play here: The hotel hopes that this promotion will put it over the edge for reaching high occupancy, and in turn, lead to higher reimbursement for all redemptions over those peak nights While redeeming points is a great value in the first place (compared to the cash rate), the reality is that hotels are increasingly trying to skim the market, so they’d rather keep very high cash rates with a large percentage of rooms booked with points, rather than just lowering the cash rates This promotion is (smartly) being offered after the cancelation deadline for most rate types at the hotel, so people with existing bookings won’t be able to take advantage of this The Park Hyatt Beaver Creek is encouraging points redemptions Bottom line The Park Hyatt Beaver Creek is offering 15,000 points per night for award redemption over peak holiday dates. So while the standard rate is 55,000 points per night, you’d end up paying 40,000 points per night, which is quite the deal compared to the cash rate. Given that some hotels treat points guests as second class guests who are staying for “free,” I think the goal here is pretty clear. Hotels are reimbursed for award stays based on overall occupancy levels, and presumably the hotel hopes that a promotion like this will get it to the occupancy level needed to trigger the highest reimbursement rate. What do you make of this Park Hyatt Beaver Creek promotion?

title: Amex Blue Business Card Bonus: As High As 50K Points Or $500 Cash Back Welcome Offer
summary: Amex has boosted welcome offers on the Blue Business Plus (up to 50,000 points) and Blue Business Cash (up to $500), both with no annual fee.
content: At the moment, we’re seeing increased welcome offers on two of Amex’s most lucrative business cards — The Blue Business® Plus Credit Card from American Express and The American Express Blue Business Cash® Card. Ordinarily these cards have really unremarkable bonuses, but at the moment the offers have been improved very nicely — we’re talking doubled on one card, and more than tripled on the other card. If you don’t yet have either card, this is absolutely the time to apply. I’ll cover the welcome offer on the Amex Blue Business Plus, which I’d argue is one of Amex’s most lucrative and most approachable business cards, especially for those looking to accrue points. I’ll also talk about the Amex Blue Business Cash, which is essentially the cash back version of the card. Link: Learn more about The Blue Business® Plus Credit Card from American Express and The American Express Blue Business Cash® Card What is the current Amex Blue Business Plus welcome offer? The Amex Blue Business Plus Card bonus is currently as high as 50,000 Membership Rewards points after spending $5,000 on purchases within the first three months of card membership. Apply and find out your welcome offer. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer. Based on my latest miles & points valuations , Amex Membership Rewards points are worth 1.7 cents each, potentially making this offer worth $850. As a point of comparison, previously the publicly available welcome offer was just 15,000 points after spending $3,000 within the first three months, so this offer is potentially worth more than three times as much. For a no annual fee card ( Rates & Fees ), this is pretty incredible. This is absolutely the time to apply if you’re interested. However, as I’ll explain below, the reason you get the card isn’t just because of the welcome offer, but also because of the long term value that it offers. There are lots of great uses of Amex Membership Rewards points , as they can be transferred to all kinds of useful airline and hotel partners, ranging from Air Canada Aeroplan, to Air France-KLM Flying Club, to Singapore Airlines KrisFlyer, to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club. Just to give some examples of how points could be redeemed: You could transfer 60,000 points to Flying Blue to book a one-way Air France business class award from Miami (MIA) to Paris (CDG), with $336.90 in taxes & fees; that same flight would cost thousands of dollars if paying cash You could transfer 60,000 points to Aeroplan to book a one-way SWISS business class award from Boston (BOS) to Zurich (ZRH), with $56.62 in taxes & fees; that same flight would cost thousands of dollars if paying cash Transfer Amex points to Flying Blue for an Air France business award Redeem Amex points for Air France business class Who is eligible for the Amex Business Plus welcome offer? In line with Amex’s “once in a lifetime” rule , the Amex Blue Business Plus Card bonus isn’t available to those who currently have the card, or those who have had the card (or previous versions of the card) in the past. On top of that, Amex’s general card restrictions apply. There are a few additional things to note : You are eligible for the Amex Blue Business Plus bonus if you’ve had any other Amex card, so you can apply for this card even if you have another Amex business card Amex typically has a limit of letting someone have at most five Amex credit cards (including personal and business cards), and this card does count toward that limit, unlike some other Amex business cards If you’re worried about the Chase 5/24 limit , getting approved for the Amex Blue Business Plus shouldn’t count as a further card toward that limit Amex does sometimes have application pop-ups indicating that you may not be eligible for a welcome offer even though you meet the published requirements otherwise, and in those cases there’s not much you can do Anecdotally, I find Amex business cards to generally be among the easiest to get approved for . I also want to emphasize that Amex business cards not counting toward the 5/24 limit really makes the opportunity cost of picking up this card pretty low, for those of us into maximizing our rewards. Many will be eligible for the welcome offer on the card Why the Amex Business Plus Card is a no-brainer The first thing to love about the Amex Blue Business Plus Card is that it has no annual fee ( Rates & Fees )… you can’t beat that! But really what makes this card unrivaled within the Amex ecosystem is its return on spending, up to a certain limit. Specifically, the Amex Blue Business Plus offers 2x Membership Rewards points on the first $50,000 spent every calendar year, and then 1x points. It’s that straightforward. So $50,000 in spending per year would earn you 100,000 Membership Rewards points. This is the only no annual fee credit card on the market that earns 2x transferable points that can be moved to the full list of airline and hotel partners at the “premium” ratio. There’s literally not another card like that. The one caveat is that the card does have foreign transaction fees, so I wouldn’t recommend using it for purchases abroad ( Rates & Fees ). Speaking of the ability to move points to partners, I think that gets at the other thing that’s awesome about the Amex Blue Business Plus Card — in the event that you want to close other Amex cards (with annual fees) that accrue Membership Rewards points, this is a great card to have, so that you can maintain your points balance, given the ability to pool points. So I view this as a very low risk card to apply for, especially with it not counting toward Chase’s 5/24 limit. The only reason I wouldn’t get this card is if I’m otherwise at the Amex five credit card limit. Read a full review of the Amex Blue Business Plus Card here . Earning up to 2x points on everyday spending is great The Amex Blue Business Cash is the cash back equivalent In the Blue Business portfolio, the Amex Blue Business Plus Card is the standout card for me. However, I should also mention the Amex Blue Business Cash Card , which is essentially the cash back equivalent: The Amex Blue Business Cash welcome offer is as high as a $500 statement credit after spending $5,000 on purchases within the first three months of card membership; apply and find out your welcome offer, as welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer The Amex Blue Business Cash is considered independently from the Blue Business Plus in terms of eligibility and earning the welcome offer The Amex Blue Business Cash offers 2% cash back on the first $50,000 spent every calendar year, and then 1% cash back after that The Amex Blue Business Cash also has no annual fee ( Rates & Fees ), so there’s limited downside to holding onto it Personally, I get more excited by the Amex Blue Business Plus Card than the Amex Blue Business Cash Card, simply because I value Amex points at well over one cent each. That’s why I’d rather earn 2x points rather than 2% cash back. Admittedly, not everyone will feel the same, especially those who don’t actually want to put the effort into maximizing points. The Amex Blue Business Cash bonus is also greatly improved, though, as it was previously for a $250 statement credit. So this is twice as good. Read a full review of the Amex Blue Business Cash Card here . Amex Blue Business Card bonus FAQs What is the highest bonus offer for the Amex Blue Business Plus? The highest publicly available welcome offer on the Amex Blue Business Plus is currently as high as 50,000 bonus Membership Rewards points upon completing minimum spending. This is the best publicly available welcome offer that we’ve seen on the card in a very long time. What is the highest bonus offer for the Amex Blue Business Cash? The highest publicly available welcome offer on the Amex Blue Business Cash is currently as high as $500 statement credit upon completing minimum spending. This is among the best publicly available welcome offers that we’ve seen on the card. What is the difference between the Amex Blue Business Plus & Amex Blue Business Cash? The Amex Blue Business Plus offers 2x Membership Rewards points on the first $50,000 spent every calendar year (then 1x points), while the Amex Blue Business Cash offers 2% cash back on the first $50,000 spent every calendar year (then 1% cash back). Can you earn the bonus if you product change to the Amex Blue Business Plus? The Amex Blue Business Plus welcome offer is only available to those who directly apply for the card. If you product change from another Amex card, you’re generally not eligible for the bonus. Is the Amex Blue Business Plus worth it? Personally, I think it’s hard to go wrong with a no annual fee card that earns 2x transferable points per dollar spent, especially when it’s a card that can “preserve” your balance of points, if you close down other products in the Amex ecosystem. Bottom line The Amex Blue Business Plus Card is a product that often flies under the radar. Ordinarily the card doesn’t have a very exciting bonus, but at the moment, we’re seeing a much better opportunity than usual. The card has a welcome offer as high as 50,000 bonus Membership Rewards points. Getting a no annual fee card that earns 2x transferable points (on the first $50,000 spent annually, then 1x points) that can be moved directly to airline and hotel partners at the most favorable ratio is something you won’t find on any other card. That’s why this card is in my wallet, and the welcome offer is just the icing on the cake. Meanwhile if you’re looking for the cash back equivalent, it’s at least worth mentioning the Amex Blue Business Cash Card , which has a bonus as high as $500 cash back as a statement credit. That no annual fee card earns 2% cash back (on the first $50,000 spent annually, then 1% cash back), also with no annual fee. These are both really lucrative cards that can be worth holding onto in the long run, so if you’re eligible, I’d absolutely recommend applying. Anyone else love the Amex Blue Business Plus Card , and think it’s an underrated option in the Amex portfolio?
